title: §01-012: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything
description: Active recall flashcards for §01-012: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything.

cards.question: In modern React 19 applications, what is the core architectural principle governing Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything?

options.text: Declarative component functions return virtual tree descriptions that React Fiber reconciles against host DOM nodes.
Components imperatively manipulate the browser DOM directly via querySelector and innerHTML mutations.
State changes bypass the reconciliation phase to trigger synchronous full-page document reloads.
All component functions must run in the global window scope as unbundled script tags.

cards.explanation: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything adheres to React's declarative mental model: components express UI state transformations as pure projections of props and state. React Fiber schedules reconciliation and dispatches minimal batched DOM mutations.
cards.pitfall: Never reach outside the declarative model to mutate DOM nodes directly during render, as this breaks reconciliation consistency and causes hydration mismatches.

cards.concept: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything Invariants
cards.question: When dealing with Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything, what behavior occurs during the render phase?

options.text: Side effects like network calls or manual event listeners should be triggered directly within the function body.
The render phase must remain pure and free of side effects; state and prop changes trigger scheduled reconciliation passes.
Re-renders always destroy and recreate the underlying DOM subtree regardless of keys or virtual diffing.
React executes child components before calling the parent component's render function.

cards.explanation: React's render phase is strictly synchronous and pure. React may invoke render functions multiple times (e.g. in Strict Mode) to detect side effects before committing changes to the host environment.
cards.pitfall: Calling dispatchers or running asynchronous promises directly in the component body produces infinite render loops or memory leaks.
cards.citation: React 19 Learn: Describing the UI & Keeping Components Pure

cards.concept: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything Execution
cards.question: How should TypeScript interfaces be structured when implementing Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything?

options.text: Use 'any' for all props to bypass strict checking and facilitate rapid prototyping.
Define explicit, read-only interfaces/types with discrimination where applicable to guarantee compile-time verification.
Attach arbitrary properties directly to the window object to share data across modules.
Disable strictNullChecks in tsconfig.json so undefined properties are silently coerced to null.

cards.explanation: Strict TypeScript types ensure that components and state hooks adhere to explicit compile-time contracts. Read-only properties reflect the immutable nature of React props.
cards.pitfall: Mutating incoming props directly violates component purity and causes silent desynchronization bugs.
cards.citation: TypeScript Handbook: Interfaces and Readonly Properties

cards.concept: Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything Edge Cases
cards.question: What is the most common production pitfall encountered when working with Prediction: A Root Component That Does Everything?

options.text: Stale closures, omission of exhaustive dependencies, or impure mutations causing cache inconsistencies.
Using functional components instead of legacy class components with componentDidMount.
Compiling TypeScript with Vite rather than webpack 4.
Writing components in separate .tsx files rather than a single monolithic script.

cards.explanation: In modern React, stale closures and omitting dependencies from hook dependency arrays or store selectors lead to stale data bugs. Always use the exhaustive-deps lint rule and maintain pure updater functions.
cards.pitfall: Direct in-place array or object mutation (e.g. array.push()) fails shallow equality checks and prevents components from re-rendering.
cards.citation: React 19 Official Documentation: Avoiding Direct State Mutation
